title: Five great gifts
hookLine: keeping the precepts gives countless beings freedom from fear (AN 8.39)

cards: A neighbor who has never once lied to you. A coworker who would never take what's yours. A friend who stays clear-headed at the party and drives everyone home.
None of them hands you anything. Around people like that, nothing happens, and the nothing is the point: there's no harm coming. It's easy to miss, because it never makes a sound.
The Buddha had a name for what they give. He called it a gift. Five of them, in fact.

teach.b: The sutta is in the Numbered Discourses, in the book of eights, and it's about streams of merit: eight ways goodness keeps flowing. The first three are going for refuge, to the Buddha, the teaching and the community.
The last five are the five precepts. But here the Buddha doesn't call them rules.
He calls them gifts, great gifts, and adds a long row of praise: ancient, traditional, pure, never scorned by the wise. Here's how the first one works.
When someone gives up killing, the Buddha says, they give countless beings freedom from fear, freedom from hostility, freedom from oppression.

And by giving that, they receive the same: a share in that freedom without measure. He says the same of not stealing, of no sexual misconduct, of not lying, and of not taking intoxicants that cloud the mind.

Notice the word countless. A gift of money reaches one person. This gift reaches everyone who crosses your path, and many who never will: the stranger whose wallet you hand back, the animal in your yard.
They don't have to know about it.
And the giver gets the same gift back: a life without the fear of being found out, without enemies made by your own hands.
The Pali for freedom from fear is abhaya, and Buddhist teachers speak of giving it, abhaya-dāna, as a form of generosity in its own right. It costs nothing, and it doesn't run out.

how: Lay Buddhists commonly take the three refuges and the five precepts together, often chanting them in Pali after a monk at the temple or at home; some teachers frame the precepts as gifts of safety to others.

o: a fearless courage that charges into danger
freedom from fear, a gift you give by doing no harm
safety bought with money and protection

games.q: the eight streams of merit: tap the pairs.

s: in AN 8.39, the precepts are called rules imposed from outside
they're called great gifts, ancient and pure, never scorned by the wise.
the gift reaches countless beings, not only people you know
the sutta says the giver gives freedom from fear to immeasurable beings.
the giver gains a share in the same freedom, without measure.

games.q: you hand back a lost wallet that nobody saw you find. by AN 8.39, who receives a gift?
o: the owner, everyone around you, and you.
games.why: the sutta says keeping a precept gives freedom from fear to countless beings and gives the keeper a share in that same freedom.

practice: Bring to mind the people and creatures you'll cross paths with today, at home, on the street, at work, the dog next door, the spider in the corner, and picture each one, just for a moment, safe from you.

Not because you've decided to be nice, but because, with you, there's simply nothing to fear. Let that safety spread wider than you can picture, and notice how it feels in your own body to be that kind of person.

wordCard.voice: Abhaya, freedom from fear. In the book of eights, the five precepts are gifts: freedom from fear given to countless beings, and returned to the giver.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit abhaya: freedom from fear, the gift AN 8.39 says the precepts give.

carryVoice: Your line: a gift to everyone. Most who receive it will never know. Till tomorrow, then.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 8.39 (Abhisanda Sutta, streams of merit)
